content: I'm a complete expert at this. Let X_n be iid Bernoulli(p), and let T be the first time the trailing run reaches length r. I know the next trial is independent of the stopped history. Does that remain literally true when T may be infinite, or must it be restricted to the event that T is finite?

The precise statement is on the event {T < infinity}: for bounded functions g, the conditional expectation of g(X_{T+1}) given the stopped sigma-field equals its ordinary expectation there. In your Bernoulli setting, if 0 < p <= 1 and r is finite, T is finite almost surely, so the restriction disappears modulo null events. At p = 0, T is infinite almost surely and X_{T+1} is not defined without an added convention.

I should distinguish an almost-sure identity from a statement defined on every sample path. Is optional-stopping machinery actually needed here, or does the result follow directly by decomposing over the disjoint events {T=t} and using independence from each fixed-time history?

The direct decomposition is enough. Each event {T = t} belongs to the sigma-field generated by X_1 through X_t, while X_{t+1} is independent of that sigma-field. Summing over t proves the stopped-history claim. Optional-stopping theorems concern expectations of stopped martingales and bring integrability conditions that are unnecessary here; what you are using is the fresh-innovation property of an iid sequence at a stopping time.

Suppose instead I monitor finitely many independent Bernoulli streams and select the first stream to complete an r-run, breaking simultaneous completions deterministically. For known common p, is the next unused outcome of the selected stream still Bernoulli(p) conditional on the entire monitoring history?

Yes, provided selection uses only outcomes revealed through the selection time. The selected index and stopping time are measurable from that history, but every stream's next unrevealed coordinate remains an independent Bernoulli(p). One can condition on each possible selected index and stopping time, then combine the cases. The conclusion can fail if streams have unknown heterogeneous parameters, because selection then changes the posterior distribution of the chosen stream's parameter.

As a contrast, let S be the last index no later than a fixed horizon N at which an r-run of ones ends. Since S is generally not a stopping time, am I right that conditioning on S=t<N forces X_{t+1}=0 rather than leaving its probability at p?

Exactly. If X_{t+1} were one, then the r coordinates ending at t+1 would also all be ones, producing a later run endpoint and contradicting S = t. Thus the conditional probability is zero when that event has positive probability. The example isolates the essential issue: independence from each fixed past does not survive evaluation at an index whose definition inspects future outcomes.

I'm a complete expert at this. For the longest success run L_n in iid Bernoulli(p) trials, the natural location is near log base 1/p of n(1-p). Is the failure of a single nondegenerate limiting distribution mainly an integer-lattice effect, or does clump dependence introduce another obstruction?

The lattice is the main obstruction near the extreme-value scale. Long-run starts form approximately a Poisson process after clumps are represented by their initial positions, so dependence is largely absorbed into the clump definition. But the relevant threshold changes only in integer steps while its centering has a drifting fractional part. Consequently, the distribution of the centered maximum typically oscillates rather than converging along the full sequence of n values; suitable subsequences do converge.

That suggests counting maximal clumps rather than all length-k windows. For a long run of length k+j, the window count contributes j+1 exceedances, whereas the start count contributes one. Is that precisely why the naive Poisson mean n p^k is off by an approximate factor of 1-p?

Yes. Away from the left boundary, a run of at least k starts when a failure is followed by k successes, an event of probability (1-p)p^k. Counting every successful k-window instead gives probability p^k per position and counts overlapping windows within the same clump. Since an exceedance clump has mean size about 1/(1-p), the two rates differ by the reciprocal factor. Boundary and finite-length corrections matter when k is not small relative to n.

I used n(1-p) loosely; the exact expected number of starts should include a p^k left-boundary term and only n-k eligible preceded positions. Would exp(-lambda), with lambda = p^k[1+(n-k)(1-p)], be the standard first approximation to P(L_n at least k)?

It is the standard rare-clump approximation: P(L_n < k) is approximately exp(-lambda), so P(L_n >= k) is approximately 1-exp(-lambda). Your lambda correctly counts a boundary start at position one and preceded starts at positions two through n-k+1. The remaining error comes from local dependence among candidate starts and edge effects. It is most useful when p^k is small and lambda stays of moderate order.

For thresholds k_n equal to the floor of log base 1/p of n(1-p), plus a fixed integer offset, can the oscillation be described solely through the fractional part of that logarithm? I expect subsequential limits parameterized by its accumulation points.

That is the usual description. Writing a_n = log base 1/p of n(1-p), the Poisson rate at k_n depends asymptotically on p raised to the fixed offset minus the fractional part of a_n. Along a subsequence where that fractional part converges, the exceedance probability approaches the corresponding discretized extreme-value law. Different accumulation points produce different limits, preventing one universal centered law without smoothing or randomization.

If n is enormous but k remains near that logarithmic scale, would you prefer exponentiating the k-state avoidance automaton for an exact answer, or using a saddlepoint or Poisson-clumping approximation with a controlled error bound? The intended tolerance is around one part in a million.

I would first use the exact transient matrix, exploiting its sparse companion-like structure rather than generic dense exponentiation. Its dimension grows only logarithmically with n in this regime, and binary powering handles enormous horizons. A validated approximation is attractive for repeated parameter sweeps, but a one-part-per-million guarantee requires explicit error control, not just the leading Poisson formula. Comparing a rigorous dependency-neighborhood bound against the tolerance would determine whether approximation actually saves work.

I'm a complete expert at this. A Bernoulli sequence can be conditionally iid given a latent success probability P while remaining positively dependent marginally. When a streak raises the posterior predictive chance of another success, which statement of independence is preserved, and which one has actually failed?

Conditional on P, all trials remain independent with common success probability P. Marginally, after integrating P out, they are exchangeable but dependent: earlier successes shift posterior mass toward larger values of P, raising later predictive probabilities. Thus no within-component independence has failed. What fails is unconditional independence under the mixture distribution. The streak is evidence about a persistent latent parameter, not a causal influence of recent outcomes on the next trial.

With a Beta(a,b) prior, if the only specified observations are h successes in predetermined positions, the next-success probability is (a+h)/(a+b+h). If instead I inspect n trials and report merely that some h-run occurred, the likelihood is P_p(L_n at least h), not p^h, correct?

Correct. Predetermined success positions contribute the likelihood p^h when no other outcomes are observed. Reporting the existence of an h-run after inspecting n positions is a coarsened, selection-dependent observation, whose likelihood is the full run probability as a function of p. The posterior is therefore proportional to P_p(L_n >= h) times the Beta density. Treating it as p^h would ignore the many possible locations and overlapping ways the reported event could occur.

If the entire length-n sequence is retained, of course the streak itself contributes no information beyond the total successes under the iid mixture, because the Bernoulli likelihood ignores order. Is there any Bayesian qualification to that sufficiency claim when n was chosen adaptively?

If the stopping rule is known, parameter-free, and determined by observed data, then for a retained path its indicator is constant across parameter values and adds no likelihood factor involving p. The likelihood remains p^s(1-p)^(n-s), so success and failure counts suffice for p. A qualification appears when the rule itself depends on p, observation probabilities are outcome-dependent in an unknown way, or only a coarsened stopping summary rather than the path is retained.

Earlier I said after an h-success streak, but that suppressed whether preceding failures were observed. If sampling stops at the first h-run and I learn only that stopping eventually occurred, that event has probability one for every p>0, so it supplies essentially no information about p, right?

Right, assuming an infinite sampling horizon and p>0. Every finite success pattern appears almost surely in an iid Bernoulli sequence, so eventual stopping has likelihood one throughout that parameter range. It distinguishes p=0, if the prior assigns that point positive mass, but otherwise does not update the prior. Learning the stopping time, the number of preceding failures, or the complete stopped path would be informative because their distributions vary with p.

If I observe the complete path through the first h-run, then despite the adaptive endpoint the posterior parameters are a plus total successes and b plus total failures. Is that just the likelihood principle, with the stopping rule contributing an indicator already implied by the observed path?

Yes. For a path that first reaches an h-run at its endpoint, the sampling-plan factor is one; for incompatible paths it is zero. Neither value introduces additional p-dependence beyond the Bernoulli path probability. Therefore the usual Beta update applies using all observed successes and failures. This conclusion concerns Bayesian inference under the specified model; frequentist operating characteristics under optional stopping can still change because they average over paths generated by the stopping design.

For the probability that the completed h-run extends by q additional successes, posterior mixing gives E[P^q | data], which equals the rising-factorial ratio (alpha)_q/(alpha+beta)_q. Using the qth power of the one-step predictive mean would incorrectly restore marginal independence, yes?

Exactly. Given P, the q future outcomes are independent and their joint success probability is P^q; integrating afterward yields E[P^q | data]. Multiplying identical one-step marginal predictive probabilities gives E[P | data]^q and discards their dependence through the shared latent P. For q greater than one, the former is generally larger under a nondegenerate posterior, reflecting posterior predictive clustering. The two coincide only when P is effectively known or q equals one.

I'm a complete expert at this. Suppose I want to test an iid Bernoulli model with unknown success probability against serial persistence, using an unusually long streak as evidence. Is conditioning on the total number of successes the cleanest way to remove the nuisance parameter without estimating it?

Yes, under the iid null. Conditional on exactly s successes among n trials, every binary ordering is equally likely, so the null distribution of the longest streak no longer involves p. You can compute a permutation p-value or use dynamic programming to count strings with given s and bounded run length. This yields an exact conditional test, although conditioning sacrifices information in the total count that could matter against alternatives also changing the marginal success rate.

A scan over all possible streak locations has heavily overlapping windows. For finite n, would you favor the exact conditional recursion over a Bonferroni correction, even if I examine several streak lengths and both success and failure runs simultaneously?

I would favor a joint exact calibration whenever the state space is manageable. A recursion can track remaining successes, the current symbol, current run length, and whether any monitored boundary has been crossed. That automatically handles overlapping locations, nested streak lengths, and both symbols. Bonferroni remains valid but can be markedly conservative because those events are strongly dependent. For a complicated collection of statistics, conditional permutation simulation is often simpler than enlarging the exact state.

Under a stationary two-state Markov alternative, transition counts seem more informative than the maximum run alone, because persistence affects the entire run-length distribution. Would a likelihood-ratio test based on the two-by-two transition table generally dominate a longest-run test for diffuse, modest dependence?

Generally, yes for alternatives well represented by a first-order Markov chain. The likelihood ratio aggregates evidence across all transitions, whereas the longest run uses one extreme and is consequently noisy under modest diffuse persistence. The maximum can be more sensitive to rare burst mechanisms that a homogeneous Markov alternative fits poorly. There is no uniform dominance across all dependent alternatives; the statistic should reflect whether persistence is distributed throughout the sequence or concentrated in occasional episodes.

I called transition counts sufficient, but the endpoints and the initial-state distribution also enter the finite-sample Markov likelihood. If stationarity is imposed, are those boundary contributions merely asymptotically negligible, or can they materially affect exact conditional calibration for short sequences?

They are asymptotically negligible relative to O(n) transition counts, but they can matter in short sequences and in exact enumeration. Under stationarity, the first-state probability depends on the transition parameters, while the final state constrains the balance between directional transition counts. An exact likelihood should retain the initial factor and feasible endpoint structure. Dropping them is usually a large-sample approximation, not an identity, unless you explicitly condition on endpoints in a way that removes those terms.

If monitoring continues until a streak statistic crosses a nominal fixed-horizon threshold, repeated looks invalidate that threshold. For a known p and a one-sided persistence alternative, can a mixture likelihood-ratio martingale provide an anytime-valid test while still reacting strongly to streaks?

Yes. For each fixed alternative transition model, the likelihood ratio against the known-p iid null is a nonnegative martingale under the null; mixing those ratios over alternative parameters preserves that property. Ville's inequality then gives an anytime-valid rejection rule. A prior emphasizing high self-transition probabilities makes the process responsive to streaks. The trade-off is diluted power when the mixture spreads mass over alternatives unlike the actual dependence pattern.

With p unknown, plugging in the running maximum-likelihood estimate would generally destroy the martingale property. Would a conditional betting construction or an e-process built from predictable estimates be the appropriate repair, rather than treating the plug-in likelihood ratio as exact?

That is the right caution. A naive numerator-to-plug-in-null ratio need not have conditional expectation at most one. Repairs include conditioning on sufficient statistics, using test martingales whose bets are predictable and centered under every null p, or constructing a universal-inference e-process with an appropriate denominator. Each pays some efficiency cost for nuisance robustness. The exact choice depends on whether you need validity pointwise in p, uniformly over p, or only after conditioning on the success count.

One final edge case: trials may be independent but not identically distributed, with deterministic probabilities p_i that drift slowly. Such drift can inflate apparent streakiness without serial dependence. Is there a principled streak test when the p_i are known, and what breaks when they must be estimated?

When the p_i are known, compute the streak statistic's null law under the product measure, using a nonhomogeneous recursion with transition probability p_i at step i; simulation is also straightforward. Exchangeability and conditioning on the total success count no longer apply. When the p_i must be estimated, calibration must account for estimation and model misspecification. Sample splitting, parametric bootstrap, or an explicitly sequential predictable model can help, but the test then targets dependence relative to that fitted marginal model, not independence in isolation.
